AQUA calculates the properties of cross sections of any shape and made out of any material. The cross section properties for a static analysis are determined, as well as characteristic magnitudes for the calculation of normal and shear stresses. Cross sections need to be defined before input of the static system or the dimensioning with AQB.
 After definition with AQUA, the cross sections can be represented graphically with Re- sultViewer.

All static properties of cross sections are directly specified. This includes shear deformation areas and stress resistance values. The values may be taken from other cross sections with a multiplication factor. These cross sections are mainly used in the static calculations. Their usage in AQB is strongly restricted.

A standard cross section (Rolled steel shapes, Rectangle, I-beam, annular sections, cables) is always defined with a single command. All cross sectional properties, including the torsional moment of inertia, are available. Due to the known geometric structure, most of the property values may be calculated in a direct way, allowing to skip the time consuming detailed analysis of the shear or plastic resistance only available with an AQUA license. In many cases it is also intended to have these simpler values taken from tabulated data in the literature. On the other side variability and locations of design points are thus limited. A detailed analysis or a combination with other cross section parts is only possible for the rolled steel shapes.
 Thus all other sections do not allow neither the calculation of von Mises stresses nor the design for fatigue.

A freely defined thin-walled cross section may contain any number of thin elements, whose thickness is much smaller comparative to its length. A thin element assumes that the variation of the normal stress and most shear stresses over the thickness are negligible. This has the consequence that the moment of inertia about the weak axis also vanishes. Available elements are panels, standard steel shapes and welded joints, as well as reinforcements.
 Section moduli for all stresses are available at all points of the cross section. Torsional moment of inertia and warping resistance, as well as centre of shear and shear deformation areas, are determined for open or closed shapes, but they can also be specified explicitly for special cases. Composite cross sections can be defined.

A freely defined solid cross section consists of any number of outer and inner perimeters in the form of circles or polygons, as well as of reinforcement elements. Structural steel shapes can be integrated.
 Section moduli for all stresses are only available at distinct points of the cross section. The torsional moment of inertia, the centre of shear and the shear deformation areas can be calcu- lated, or they can be input separately. The warping resistance can not be determined. Com- posite sections or effective widths of the polygons can be defined.

A freely defined FE cross section will be imported from a FE mesh available in a separate external data base. Stress points, reinforcement elements or shear cuts may be added then. The import may also activate a temperature field for the section (e.g. hot design).
 All sectional values including warping are evaluated. Section moduli for all forces and moments are available for all element mid points. Composite sections may be defined.

The user has to decide on his own authority, which type of sectional description to choose. Due to the established restrictions a standard cross section may have more sectional data available than a poorly defined general cross section.
 A thin walled section has much in common with a standard frame analysis, while the solid section requires a continua solution. This means that the simplifications of the thin walled approach allow a faster, more robust and more extensive solution, but neglects local effects, which may become visible within a continua solution with integral equations or finite elements.
 For example it is to be noted, that for a thin hollow box, the shear stress of the continua solution is not really constant across the web thickness and may have higher intensities at the corners which might require a smoothing of the contour. On the other side a thin walled section has problems to take account of the positive effect of the fillets of a thin rolled steel shape which has a considerable contribution to the torsional strength.
 The checks for the c/t ratio for steel sections are much more easily performed with a thin walled section and the modelling of discrete dowels is only possible with this type of approach.
 In general problems have to be expected if a section is not modelled with the optimum method. Especially very thin plates with stiffeners modelled as polygons need a very high numerical effort.

Due to the fact that most cross sections are build up according to certain rules, AQUA supplies several definition possibilities for these instances:
 ¢ You may describe the section via CADINP variables within a block, which is then used multiple times.
 ¢ You may interpolate between two sections linearly
 ¢« You can define a cross section template consisting of several construction points. Other points are referenced hierarchically to those original points. You can then generate other cross sections by changing these points.
 * You may describe the position of those construction points by a 3D model with curved reference lines.
 It is also possible for AQUA to update all interpolated or otherwise generated sections with a single command (INTE).

Properties of materials must be distinguished according to whether they are to be kept as close as possible to real values (e.g. for dynamic calculations) or to be used with a safety coefficient for calculating an ultimate load-bearing capacity.
 A small, but subtle contradiction is given by the fact, that many design codes use a factor of 10.0 to convert the density of a material [t/m?] to the weight [kN/m?]. The US customary units use the pound as base unit, the masses are converted with a nominal value of the gravity acceleration.
 To avoid any confusion and to use all the benefits of the Sl-System SOFISTiK has established the following rules:
 All specified weights have to be specified in (kN/m3) or (lb/ft3), but they are saved as masses to the data base. Thus a direct definition of the mass with a unit of (kg/m3) or (lbm/ft3) is also possible.
 ¢
 ¢ Masses for dynamic or densities for thermal analysis will be always determined directly from that data.
 ¢ If the design code or the user allows for more precise loadings, the user may specify the true value of the gravity acceleration for the reference location with the NORM record.
 Somehow confusing, there is an additional density value of the raw material. This value is relevant for many physical properties of concrete or timber, but its value is less than the value used for self weight.
 Whereas the safety factors were formerly assigned more-or-less at random, sometimes to the load and sometimes to the material, more recent regulations (Eurocode) provide a clearer separation between safety factors for the loads and factors for the material.
 Since the material safety factors still depend on the nature of the load or the type of design, AQUA generates and stores only the genuine properties of the material. However, AQUA accounts for some safety factors which are independent of the particular loading case, such as long term reduction factors.

Whereas the safety factors were formerly assigned more-or-less at random, sometimes to the load and sometimes to the material, more recent regulations (Eurocode) provide a clearer separation between safety factors for the loads and factors for the material.. Since the material safety factors still depend on the nature of the load or the type of design, AQUA generates and stores only the genuine properties of the material. However, AQUA accounts for some safety factors which are independent of the particular loading case, such as long term reduction factors..
 Nevertheless, a safety coefficient can be entered in AQUA for each material; this is used in AQUA for calculating the full plastic section forces and moments, and can be used in AQB for the strain checks.

Any type of hole will be generated automatically if polygons or circles overlap. A true hole is now defined with material number 0. To avoid any ambiguities, some rules have to be followed however:
 ¢ A polygon/circle may create a hole in another area only if it has a different material number and at least one vertex of the periphery within the other area. The latter is only true provided that the edges of the two polygons maintain a minimum distance of 0.5 [mm] apart.
 ¢ Ifa polygon/circle is completely within another area, it will always create a hole, if the areas overlap partly the sequence of the input will decide: The area defined last will be considered ”in front of” and will create a hole in the area laying behind.

The image is a three-dimensional schematic of a prismatic beam element with its local coordinate systems and key sectional points marked. The beam is drawn as a long rectangular bar, oriented so that its longitudinal (x-) axis runs from left to right between two solid black “node” spheres—one at each end. The viewer is looking toward the positive face of a cut section at the right-hand end of the beam.

Along the length of the beam, a dashed centerline indicates the local x-axis. At the right-hand cut face:
 • An arrow labeled “N” emerges from the face, pointing horizontally to the right. This represents the axial (normal) force along the local x-axis.
 • Two thick black arrows originate near the lower front corner of the cut face: one pointing downward, labeled “Mz” (the bending moment about the y-axis), and one pointing diagonally off toward the left and slightly into the page, labeled “My” (the bending moment about the z-axis).
 • A small red dot on the face is annotated with “S.” This dot marks the Elastic Reference Point (also referred to as the gross-section centroid for a homogeneous section), which serves as the origin of the sectional y–z coordinate system for bending and axial-force calculations.

On the vertical left face of the beam (a second imaginary cut), a second small red dot appears, and the local sectional axes y′s and z′s are drawn: y′s is horizontal and pointing to the left, z′s is vertical and pointing downward. These primed axes indicate the principal axes of the section shifted to the elasticity-weighted center (minimizing the second moment of area about one axis).

Across the right-hand face, the unprimed axes y and z define the standard local sectional system: y horizontally toward the observer’s lower-left and z vertically downward. The z-axis is explicitly identified as the “main bending direction” and is shown aligned with gravity (downward).

Labels and line conventions:
 • Solid straight arrows denote force and moment directions (N, My, Mz).
 • Thin solid arrows without force labels define local coordinate axes.
 • Dashed lines and a long centerline show the beam’s x-axis and the relationship between nodes.
 • Black spheres denote the end nodes of the beam element.
 • Red spheres mark sectional reference points: on the right face the Elastic Reference (S); on the left cut the shifted principal-axis center (y′s, z′s).

Altogether, this figure (captioned “Figure 2.1: Coordinate system”) lays out the local beam axis (x), the cross-sectional axes (y, z and y′s, z′s), the location of the elastic reference point, and the orientation/magnitude directions of axial and bending actions. It serves to clarify how forces, moments, and centroidal points (gravity center, elastic center, shear center) are defined and located in the beam’s local coordinate system.

The image is an isometric schematic from SOFiSTiK illustrating how a beam’s local and sectional coordinate systems are defined (Figure 2.1).  At the very top sits the SOFiSTiK trademark logo (stylized blue grid‐wave with the “SOFiSTiK” wordmark).  Below it, a straight prismatic beam is drawn in three‐dimensional perspective, with two black‐filled circles marking its end nodes (one at the “start” on the upper left, one at the “end” on the lower right).  A dashed line runs longitudinally through the beam, indicating the local x-axis (“beam axis”) which connects those two nodes.  

At the right end the beam is “cut” to reveal its cross section, which in this sketch is a simple rectangular‐channel‐like shape.  From that cut face emerge two thick black arrows labeled My and Mz—the bending moments about the sectional y-axis (My, depicted as a slanted arrow pointing away from the section) and about the sectional z-axis (Mz, drawn vertically downward).  

Two distinct sectional coordinate systems are shown at the cross section:  
 • The default local section axes y and z are drawn with slender black arrows: the y-axis projects horizontally to the left, and the z-axis vertically downward (in keeping with the DIN 1080 convention of z as the main bending axis, oriented toward gravity).  
 • A shifted sectional system y′s–z′s is also depicted. Cross sections are described according to DIN 1080 in the local y-z coordinate system of the beam. Here the x-axis points in the longitudinal direction of the bar. The observer is looking in general at the positive boundary of the section (from the end of the bar to the beginning).
 The coordinate system of the section is identical with the local beam coordinate-system, i.e. the local x-axis is along the beam on the line between the nodes, the y- and the z-axis are right handed perpendicular to it. The z-axis defines the main bending direction and is in general oriented downwards in the gravity direction.
 For the description of the forces and moments and the support conditions, three points along the beam have to be distinguished within a section:
 ¢ Centre of gravity (G) - This is the physical meaning of centre and is used for the calculation of the self weight and masses.
 ¢ Elastic reference (S) - This is the centre weighted with the elasticity modulus of the gross section. For homogeneous material it is identical with the centre of gravity, thus often just named ”centre”. This value may include the basic reinforcements.
 Elastic centre (N) - This is the mechanical point where the normal force is acting. Stresses induced by a constant strain within the total section will not generate any moments refer- ence to that point. It differs from the elastic centre by the inclusion of holes and the current reinforcements. Quite often it is also called the centre of the net or ideal section.
 ¢
 ¢ Effective bending centre (B) - If some parts of the section do not take fully part due to shear deformations, this may be accounted for bei noneffective areas for bending.  ¢ Shear centre (M) - This point may be defined in several ways: A shear force acting at this point does not create torsion. A section with torsion will rotate about this point. Thus if an explicit rotation axis should be described, this point has to be defined explicitly.

   • When a cross‐section defined under the old CTRL STYP scheme is loaded in AQUA 2076, this table is consulted to remap each numeric or ranged code to its new keyword form.

The analysis with the displacement method may be also done with the Integral equation method (also termed Boundary Element Method) developed by Katz [2]. Only the cross section contour is discretized into multiple so-called “boundary elements”. A linear formulation of the warping is made for each element and the boundary condition is satisfied by a Galerkin weighted residual.

A non-vanishing solution can therefore be obtained only by defining at least four elements per side. AQUA uses each polygon edge as one element, which can be further subdivided depending on its size. Duplicate edges are automatically removed. 1) Top sketch (“Not solvable, no detached parts.”)

   – No part of the concrete cross section is intersected; there is literally “no element” on which to compute shear flow.  
   – Verdict: unsolvable because the cut does not hit any material — it lies wholly within open air.

2) Second sketch (“Solvable, the shear force is distributed right and left. Not optimal for biaxial loading.”)

   – However, these two half-cuts are not tied together, and each carries only the component of shear parallel to the cut.  
   – Verdict: mathematically solvable for shear in one direction but not optimal if the section is subject to shear about both principal axes.

3) Third sketch (“Solvable, however the contour must be located at the zero point of the shear force. Not suitable for biaxial loading.”)  
   – The horizontal red cut is the same, but a short black block is inserted at mid-span of the cut, representing a virtual or real connector at the neutral (zero-shear) line.  
   – By inserting that tie, the two half-cuts are joined into a single contiguous shear path, allowing treatment as one closed contour.  
   – The connector must be placed exactly at the shear‐flow zero location; elsewhere it would misrepresent the true flow.  
   – Verdict: permissible for a single shear direction but still fails if loads act in two perpendicular directions.

4) Fourth sketch (“Solvable, however the user must consider the component factors. Suitable for biaxial loading.”)  
   – Here the cut is a two-segment path: a horizontal red line through the inner void plus a vertical red line that up-lifts from the center of the horizontal into the top flange.  
   – Four red × markers show the endpoints of each segment. The vertical segment ensures connectivity between the bottom cavity walls and the top flange.  
   – No artificial black connector is needed, because the two segments form one continuous cut through material of the same assigned material number.  
   – By following this zig-zag or L-shaped path, shear flow from both axes can be captured, but the user must decompose the total shear force into the horizontal and vertical components and apply the corresponding section moduli or effective widths appropriately.

Overall, this figure illustrates key points from modern code procedures for equivalent hollow sections:

  • Cuts must intersect actual elements (no “open air” segments).  
  • Each partial cut segment must carry the correct material number for valid integration of shear stresses.  
  • Disconnected half-cuts can be united by virtual connectors placed at known zero‐shear locations to form a single contour.  
  • For biaxial loading, multi-leg cuts (potentially oblique or stepped) are often needed so that shear‐flow integrals cover all paths of force transmission.  
  • The width of the equivalent section and the placement of connectors control the kernel area (zero‐tension zone) and hence the required shear reinforcement.

The calculation of fully plastic forces is a very complex task. The single values for each force component may be evaluated easily, but the interaction of all forces and moments is a rather extensive numerical problem. With AQUA/AQB one has the following choices:
 ¢ Estimates for standard sections
 Plastic normal force and bending moments can be evaluated precisely. For the plastic shear force Vy, pi the plastic shear area is taken according to Eurocode including the additional fillet areas, which is a deviation from the simpler formulas given in DIN 18800 for steel shapes. For Vz,pi the fillets are ignored. For Mz; a more conservative approximation is used for thin walled sections, whereas for thick sections, the exact solution given by Backlund/Akesson is used. It should be also noted that plastic forces and moments for tabulated profiles shall always be transformed into the rotated system if the profiles are rotated around their default state.
 ¢ Evaluation of plastic forces using the real geometry (AQUA - Full Version)
 For thin walled sections of arbitrary shape and composition, the plastic normal force and bending moments are evaluated precisely. Plastic shear forces Vy 51, Vz», may be eval- uated rather well (neglecting some plastic shear centre effects). The method that AQUA currently uses for this purpose is based on scaling the elastic stresses to their yield limit, which does in the general case provide a slight, but negligible overestimation of the exact theoretical values, as in the case of Mt, pi.
 For solid sections of arbitrary shape and composition, either computed by BEM or FEM, the plastic normal force and bending moments are evaluated precisely. For torsion how- ever, it is difficult in the very general case to clearly distinguish between open and closed sections. For thick polygonal sections, a pure sum of areas would lead to significantly overestimated values for all shear problems.
 With standard BEM, as well as with FEM solely in combination with CTRL PLAS +16, AQUA will use the shear deformation area for Vy p; and Vz p1, being up to 20% on the safe side.

In reality, each resource uses a slightly different mechanical definition of the area that is to be considered as fully plastic and active. The input “Design Code” table is a master listing of all national and international structural‐engineering standards that SOFiSTiK can reference via its built-in INI‐file mechanism or special program code.  It serves two functions: first, to define which design code family and national annex applies; and second, to supply every module with the correct default material properties, load combinations, partial factors, categories, geographic inputs and boxed (“national variant”) values.  Below is a structured overview of how the table is organized and what each field means.

1. General Columns and Their Purpose  
   • Design family: an  abbreviation (e.g. EN, DIN, OEN, SIA, AS, BS, IS, US, CA, GB, NF, IT, ES, SE, DK, NO, RU, NZ, FI, NL, BE, BR, ZA) that groups a set of standards.  
   • Standard designation: the precise code number and year (e.g. EN 1992-1-1/EKS 12:2022, DIN 1045-1 (2008), OENORM B 4300 (1994)).  
   • Country code: used when the Eurocode family (EN) has boxed values or national annexes (e.g. “00” for General EN, “HK/852” for Hong Kong, “IL/972” for Israel).  
   • Category/Class (CAT): where a given code requires a usage class or safety class—values come from the matching INI‐file (for example CAT A1–A3 for Swedish building safety classes, CAT B1–B4 for Danish road bridges, or CAT LE–HR for Danish building safety/control levels).  
   • Terrain/latitude/longitude/altitude/g: optional parameters for site‐specific loads (snow, wind, seismic), where “NONE” suppresses the value; self‐weight (G) is always included unless overridden.  
   • Module support marks (A, B): indicate whether special provisions exist in AQB (A) and/or BEMESS (B) for that code.

2. INI-File Naming Convention  
   • Each combination of design family, code number and country code resolves to an INI‐file named DC_<family>_<country>.INI  
   • All numeric defaults (material fck, γM, ψ factors, combination coefficients) live there.  
   • “Boxed values” (national variant parameters inside Eurocodes) can be tweaked manually with the VAR record.

3. Special Remarks and User Guidance  
   • If actions or load cases have already been defined, re‐defining the design code may invalidate earlier defaults—this is discouraged unless only the code’s material parameters change.  
   • Historic codes without INI support (e.g. OEN 4200, 4250, 4253) still work in AQB by direct input of concrete (BOE) and steel (BSOE) properties.  
   • UNIT or dLANG records set global unit systems and languages but are only processed within AQUA or TEMPLATE; PAGE records are module-local.  
   • Users must verify that site factors (altitude, wind/snow, seismic) as applied by each module indeed meet the code’s regulations; automatic selection does not guarantee compliance.

4. Highlights of Major Families  
   – Eurocodes (EN1990–1999): with national annexes for building (SS EN199X/EKS12:2022, TSFS 2018:57 for Sweden, Transportstyrelsen for bridges) and for Denmark (DS EN1990/NA:2007, DS EN1992-2/NA:2015, etc.), each broken down by structure type (building, road bridge, footbridge, railway bridge) and safety/control classes (LE, NE, …; BNE, BHE, …; CNE, CHE, …; DNE, DHE, …).  
   – DIN and Austrian ÖNORM: concrete (DIN 1045-1 (2008), OEN B 4750 (2000)) and steel (OEN B 4300 (1994)), including Fachbericht 102. Categories A–E, etc.  
   – US and Canadian: ACI-based UBC codes, CSA S6-19 for highway bridges.  
   – Other national systems: Indian IS, Russian SP, Spanish UNE, Swiss SIA, British BS, Italian, Finnish, Netherlands (NEN), Belgian, Brazilian, South African (ZA), New Zealand (NZS).  

In summary, this table is a comprehensive registry linking every supported design standard to its exact INI file, national annex, category schema and module implementation status—all of which must be declared at the start of a project so that SOFiSTiK can load the correct defaults for geometry, materials and load combinations.

The table shown is part of the SOFiSTiK “design code” input record.  It defines a handful of global parameters—altitude, environmental zones, terrain category, plus the preferred units and language—for structural‐design modules.  Many of these values feed into default material properties, load‐combinations, snow/wind/earthquake actions and country‐specific “boxed values” in the INI‐files (e.g. DC_NDC.INI) that implement Eurocodes, DIN, ACI, BS, CSA, NZS, etc.  Changing the design code or national annex after you have already set up load cases may invalidate those defaults, so these settings should be picked at the very start of a project.

Fields:
1.  ALT  
    – Description: Altitude above mean sea level  
    – Unit: m (meters)  
    – Default: 0.0  
    – Notes: Many snow‐load combination factors, air density corrections or wind‐pressure values in national annexes depend on the site elevation.  If the true local gravity or air‐density effect is required, override the default of 0.0 m here.  If you wish to suppress any altitude‐based adjustment entirely, you may use the literal NONE (see manual).

2.  WIND  
    – Description: Wind zone  
    – Unit: Lit4 (four‐character literal)  
    – Default: * (asterisk)  
    – Notes: A code‐specific zone identifier (e.g. WZ01, ZONE, UKWB) that selects the wind map and reference wind pressure tables in the INI‐file.  If left at *, the module picks the “default” wind zone for the chosen design code (or none, if the code does not address wind).  You can explicitly set NONE to ignore wind loads.

3.  SNOW  
    – Description: Snow zone  
    – Unit: Lit4  
    – Default: *  
    – Notes: Similar to WIND.  The four‐letter code selects national snow‐load maps (e.g. SN01, ATSN) and attendant shape/combination factors.  Leaving it at * loads the code’s default or global snow map.

4.  SEIS  
    – Description: Seismic zone  
    – Unit: Lit4  
    – Default: *  
    – Notes: Four‐character seismic zone designator (e.g. Z1, ZONE, USHH).  Used by modules that implement earthquake‐resistant design (e.g. EC8 Annex or NBCC).  * picks the code’s default zone; NONE suppresses seismic actions.

5.  WCAT  
    – Description: Terrain category for wind  
    – Unit: Lit4  
    – Default: *  
    – Notes: A four‐letter code (e.g. TC1, CATD) selecting ground roughness or terrain‐category definitions for wind‐pressure calculations.  Depending on the design code and its national annex, the terrain category modifies the gust‐factor, or stability‐height functions.  * uses the default category; NONE disables terrain correction.

6.  UNIT  
    – Description: Selection of a set of units  
    – Unit: — (not applicable)  
    – Default: *  
    – Notes: This pager‐level record (only processed by AQUA or TEMPLATE) globally defines the measurement‐unit system (e.g. SI, Imperial, kN-m, lb-ft) for both input and output across all modules.  The actual unit set is defined in the matching INI‐file; * means “use the default for the selected design code.”

7.  LANG  
    – Description: Selection of an output language default  
    – Unit: —  
    – Default: *  
    – Notes: Also only picked up by AQUA/TEMPLATE.  Defines the language for printed reports, error messages and legends (e.g. EN, DE, FR, ZH).  * means “use the default language for the current design code or INI‐file.”

Usage and Overriding:  
– Any of the four‐letter fields (WIND, SNOW, SEIS, WCAT) can be set to “NONE” to suppress that particular environmental action entirely.  
– Changing ALT, WIND, SNOW, SEIS or WCAT after defining load cases may not retroactively adjust already‐generated combinations; always set at project start.  
– UNIT and LANG changes take effect globally only in AQUA or TEMPLATE; in other modules, they follow the INI defaults unless overridden in that module’s PAGE record.  
– The default asterisk (*) instructs the software to fetch the “standard” value from the chosen DC_NDC.INI file that corresponds to your design code family, country code (if EN), and language.  
– For fully custom or historic codes without INI support, you can combine design code records with VAR records to manually set any missing “boxed values.”

This table defines the complete set of input parameters needed to describe a material in a RAG-style database. It is organized into four logical blocks—basic elastic constants, anisotropic extensions, strength factors, and identification/classification—and for each parameter it lists:  
• The short “Item” code used in input files  
• A human-readable “Description”  
• The “Unit” in which the value must be supplied  
• A “Default” value or rule if the user omits it  

1. Basic Elastic and Physical Constants  
   • NO  
     – “Material number”; a simple integer index (no units); defaults to 1.  
   • E  
     – Elastic (Young’s) modulus; in MPa (reference footnote [1090]); default is inherited from material type (*) if TYPE is given.  
   • MUE  
     – Poisson’s ratio (range 0.0–0.49). For nonlinear models (NMAT), an automatic default is applied. Unitless; defaults to 0.  
   • G  
     – Shear modulus; in MPa [1090]; default drawn from TYPE.  
   • K  
     – Bulk (volumetric) modulus; in MPa [1090]; default drawn from TYPE.  
   • GAM  
     – Specific weight (unit weight in gravity field); in kN/m³ [1091]; default = 25.  
   • GAMA  
     – Submerged (buoyant) specific weight; in kN/m³ [1091]; default inherited from TYPE.  
   • ALFA  
     – Linear thermal expansion coefficient; in 1/K [1083]; default = 1×10⁻⁵.  

2. Anisotropic-Material Extensions  
   These parameters apply only when the material is modeled as transversely isotropic (plane of isotropy normal to local z):  
   • E90  
     – Elastic modulus in the transverse direction; in MPa [1090]; default = E.  
   • M90  
     – Poisson’s ratio for transverse strains; unitless; default = MUE.  
   • OAL  
     – Meridian angle of the plane of isotropy about the local x-axis; in degrees; default = 0.  
   • OAF  
     – Descent (dip) angle of the isotropic plane about x; in degrees; default = 0.  

3. Strength and Safety Factors  
   • SPM  
     – Material safety factor; unitless; default = 1.0.  
   • FY  
     – Design (allowable) strength; in MPa [1092]; no default (user must specify if relevant).  
   • FT  
     – Ultimate (failure) strength; in MPa [1092]; no default.  

4. Classification, Defaults and Labelling  
   • TYPE  
     – A literal code (LIT) that selects a predefined family of default constants. Codes include broad categories—GLAS (float or safety glass), Cu/Pb/Mg/W/Zn (metals), BRIC/CLIN/SLBR (bricks), IGYP/GYPS/MOGY (gypsum products), polymers (PVC, PEHD, PS, PP, PUR), foams, rubbers, soils (USCS codes GW, CL, MH, etc., with optional suffixes :P, :S, :H, :F to preset uniaxial strength FY based on liquidity index), and fluids (AIR, H2O, CO2, noble gases). When TYPE is given, E, G, K, MUE, GAMA and other properties marked “*” will be filled automatically.  
   • TITL  
     – Material name (up to 32 characters); purely a label, no default.  

How it ties into the user’s broader context:  
– The TYPE code drives conceptual defaults for linear elastic properties where distinct measured values are unavailable or when representing standard material families.  
– For soils, TYPE uses the Unified Soil Classification System (USCS) and the liquidity-index suffixes to preset the uniaxial compressive strength FY.  
– For fluids, TYPE sets bulk modulus K and kinematic viscosity MUE (m²/s) at standard temperature and pressure.  
– The anisotropy block plus transformation angles (OAL/OAF) allow modeling of tilted or layered geologic structures by rotating the local stiffness matrix according to the meridian and dip (Euler) angles.  

This structured parameter set ensures that every material instance in the RAG vector store is fully defined for elastic, strength, density, thermal, anisotropic, and classification aspects—whether it’s glass, metal, polymer, soil, or fluid.

Below is a structured, detailed description of the table that defines the fields for the MAT record (used to assign material‐property data for SVAL, QUAD and BRIC elements). This description can be used to populate a RAG (Retrieval‐Augmented Generation) vector store or any metadata catalog.

1. Table Overview  
• Columns  
  – Item: A short mnemonic or keyword identifying the material property.  
  – Description: Full name of the property, possibly with allowable ranges or notes.  
  – Unit: Physical units in which the property is expressed (or “–” if dimensionless).  
  – Default: The value assumed if the user does not supply one. An asterisk (*) indicates a value must be supplied or will be computed by the solver.

2. Row‐by‐Row Details  

• NO (Material number)  
  – Description: Unique integer identifier for the material.  
  – Unit: — (none)  
  – Default: 1  

• E (Elastic modulus)  
  – Description: Young’s modulus in the principal direction (linear elasticity).  
  – Unit: kN/m²  
  – Default: * (user must supply for linear analyses)  

• MUE (Poisson’s ratio)  
  – Description: Ratio of transverse to axial strain (valid range 0.0–0.49). Automatically set for nonlinear materials via the NMAT record.  
  – Unit: — (dimensionless)  
  – Default: 0  

• G (Shear modulus)  
  – Description: Material’s resistance to shear deformation; used in isotropic elasticity.  
  – Unit: kN/m²  
  – Default: * (computed from E and MUE if omitted)  

• K (Bulk modulus)  
  – Description: Volumetric stiffness, relating pressure to volumetric strain.  
  – Unit: kN/m²  
  – Default: * (computed or required for certain element types)  

• GAM (Specific weight)  
  – Description: Weight per unit volume under gravity loading.  
  – Unit: kN/m³  
  – Default: 25  

• GAMA (Specific weight under buoyancy)  
  – Description: Effective weight per unit volume when submerged/fluid‐supported.  
  – Unit: kN/m³  
  – Default: * (if not set, GAM is used)  

• ALFA (Thermal expansion coefficient)  
  – Description: Linear coefficient of thermal expansion (for temperature‐dependent strain).  
  – Unit: 1/K  
  – Default: E-5 (1×10⁻⁵ per degree K)  

• EY (Anisotropic elastic modulus Ey)  
  – Description: Young’s modulus in the secondary principal direction, for orthotropic materials.  
  – Unit: kN/m²  
  – Default: E (copies the primary E if omitted)  

• MXY (Anisotropic Poisson’s ratio m-xy)  
  – Description: Poisson’s ratio in the x–y plane for orthotropic elasticity.  
  – Unit: —  
  – Default: MUE (same as isotropic ratio if not provided)  

• OAL (Meridian angle of anisotropy about the local x-axis)  
  – Description: Rotation angle (in degrees) defining orientation of the orthotropic material’s symmetry axis.  
  – Unit: deg  
  – Default: 0°  

• OAF (Descent angle of anisotropy about the local x-axis)  
  – Description: Inclination angle (in degrees) for the orthotropic symmetry axis’s tilt.  
  – Unit: deg  
  – Default: 0°  

• SPM (Material safety factor)  
  – Description: Factor by which strength parameters are divided to ensure safety.  
  – Unit: —  
  – Default: 1.0  

• TITL (Material name)  
  – Description: Up to 32‐character text label for the material.  
  – Unit: Lit32 (text)  
  – Default: – (blank if not specified)  

3. Contextual Notes  
• MAT vs. MATE records:  
  – MAT uses kN/m² (KN/m²) units for elastic parameters, analogous to the older NMAT record. Orthotropic property names in MAT are legacy.  
  – MATE employs MPa units (like CONC, STEE) and can include additional strength values (tensile, compressive, shear strengths).  
• Numbering: Each material number (NO) must be unique across MAT and MATE definitions.  
• Defaults marked “*” are often computed internally (e.g., G and K from E and MUE) or required by the analysis engine.

The table below defines the set of input keywords you use when calling FLAY to describe a multi‐layered (up to 99 layers) composite QUAD element.  FLAY will read one layer at a time, building a stack of layer definitions whose total thickness is either scaled uniformly or adjusted selectively if relative (negative) thicknesses appear.  Each row of the table corresponds to one keyword, its semantic role, the expected unit or data format, and the default behavior if you omit that keyword on subsequent lines.

1. NO  
   • Code: NO  
   • Description: “Number of composite material”  
   • Unit / Format: — (dimensionless)  
   • Default: * (mandatory on the first layer only)  
   • Details: Identifies which composite‐stack definition you are building.  You only need to specify NO for the very first layer record.  If you omit NO on subsequent layer input lines, FLAY will reuse the last value you gave.

2. T  
   • Code: T  
   • Description: “Thickness of layer”  
   • Unit / Format: * (any positive length unit)  
   • Default: ! (mandatory for every layer)  
   • Details:  
     – A positive T gives an absolute (fixed) thickness.  
     – A negative T gives a fraction of the total, and FLAY will adjust only those relative layers to meet the overall target thickness.  
     – If all T values are positive, FLAY uniformly scales every layer so that the sum of layer thicknesses equals the element’s prescribed total thickness.

3. MNO  
   • Code: MNO  
   • Description: “Material number of layer”  
   • Unit / Format: — (integer index into your material library)  
   • Default: ! (mandatory for every layer)  
   • Details: Associates this layer with one of the pre‐defined material property sets (e.g. orthotropic lamina data).

4. BETA  
   • Code: BETA  
   • Description: “Direction of layer (angle to local x‐axis of element)”  
   • Unit / Format: — (degrees)  
   • Default: 0.0  
   • Details: Defines the fiber or principal material orientation within the plane of the layer.  If you do not supply a BETA angle, it defaults to 0° (aligned to the element’s local x‐axis).

5. TITL  
   • Code: TITL  
   • Description: “Material designation”  
   • Unit / Format: Lit32 (up to 32‐character text string)  
   • Default: – (empty)  
   • Details: An optional label or descriptive name for this composite definition.  Like NO, you only need to provide TITL once (on the first layer).  FLAY retains the last non-blank title on subsequent layers if you leave it out.

Contextual Behavior and Example  
• You may combine layers of different materials, thicknesses, and fiber orientations to reflect a sandwich or laminate construction.  
• If your total element thickness (set elsewhere in your deck) does not match the sum of the absolute T values you defined, FLAY will (a) scale all layers identically if you used only positive T’s, or (b) adjust only the negative‐valued layers if any exist, leaving the absolute layers fixed.  
• Example Use Case: A three-layer sandwich with two outer plies of fixed 1 mm thickness (T=1.0) and a foam core defined with T=–1.0 (negative to indicate “fill the remainder”) will automatically size the core so that the total stack matches the element thickness you’ve assigned.

The table shown is the definition of the “MLAY” composite‐material card used in a QUAD‐element finite‐element model.  It allows you to stack up to ten individual material layers, each with its own thickness and material identifier.  Below is a detailed, field‐by‐field description suitable for ingestion into a RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) vector store:

1.  Overall structure  
    •  Each row corresponds to one data item on the MLAY card.  
    •  Columns are:  
       –  Item: the label or keyword used in input.  
       –  Description: human‐readable explanation of the field’s purpose.  
       –  Unit: the physical or logical unit of the entry.  
       –  Default: the code or symbol indicating a required value (“!”) or optional (“–”).

2.  Item definitions  
    •  NO  
       –  “Number of composite material”  
       –  Unit: none (—)  
       –  Default: 1  
       –  Explains how many distinct composite sets will follow.  
    •  T0  
       –  “Thickness of first layer”  
       –  Unit: length (*) or a relative (negative) factor  
       –  Default: ! (required)  
    •  NO0  
       –  “Material number of first layer”  
       –  Unit: none (—)  
       –  Default: ! (required)  
    •  T1, NO1, T2, NO2, …, T9, NO9  
       –  Each Ti is the thickness of the (i+1)-th laminate.  A positive number is absolute thickness; a negative number is a relative proportion to be scaled.  
       –  Each NOi is the integer ID referencing the material definition for that layer.  
       –  Units and defaults mirror T0/NO0: thickness entries use “*”, material numbers use “—”, and most are mandatory up through layer count.  Beyond the actual number of layers you wish to specify, you may omit or leave at default (“–”).  
    •  TITL  
       –  “Material Designation”  
       –  Unit: Lit32 (a 32-character string)  
       –  Default: – (optional)  

3.  Layer‐thickness calibration logic (context)  
    –  The sum of all positive thickness values forms the “base” total thickness.  
    –  Any layer defined with a negative thickness entry will be considered “relative.”  If your composite definition contains only negative (relative) entries, each negative value is scaled so that the sum of all layers equals the requested total thickness.  
    –  If at least one layer has positive thickness, the positive‐thickness layers remain fixed and the negative layers alone are adjusted to make the total thickness match the target.  If none are negative, all positive layers are uniformly scaled.  
    –  Example (from context):  
       •  Three‐layer sandwich: upper (0.02), interior (–1.00), lower (0.02)  
       •  For a QUAD element requiring total 0.10 thickness, the interior layer becomes 0.06; for total 0.15, it becomes 0.11.  

4.  Use in non‐linear calculations  
    –  When you run a non‐linear analysis, the code stores a single “mean” or effective material definition, averaging across the calibrated layer thicknesses.  
    –  This allows the solver to handle geometric or material non‐linearities without re-interpolating every layer on each iteration.  

5.  Summary of key points for retrieval  
    –  MLAY fields: NO + up to 10×(Ti + NOi) + TITL.  
    –  Thickness entries use “*”; material IDs use “—”; TITL uses “Lit32.”  
    –  Default symbols: “!” means that entry must be provided if the layer exists; “–” means optional or not applicable.  
    –  Calibration rules distinguish absolute versus relative thickness entries and describe how the total thickness is enforced.

This table defines the input “material card” structure for a finite‐element (FE) analysis program, specifying how users select and parameterize different constitutive (material) laws.      – Default: 1

     – Description: A literal code (LIT) specifying which constitutive model to use.  This value determines both the form of the stress–strain relationship and the meaning of subsequent parameters P1…Pn.  In a purely linear analysis one may choose TYPE=LINE; if a non‐linear model is selected in a linear run, only its yield function is evaluated and reported, enabling a quick estimate of regions that would require a full non‐linear solution.  
     – Unit: LIT (literal string)  
     – Default: “!” (program prompts the user to supply a value interactively)  
   – Allowed TYPE codes and their interpretations:

     DRUC   → Drucker–Prager plasticity (optionally with viscoplastic extension)  
     MOHR   → Mohr–Coulomb plasticity  
     GRAN   → Hardening plasticity for soils (generalized Cam‐Clay, etc.)  
     SWEL   → Swelling‐shrinkage behaviour (e.g. clays with moisture effects)  
     FAUL   → Fault/slip surfaces in rock mechanics  
     ROCK   → General rock‐material model (brittle fracture, damage)  
     MISE   → Combined von Mises/Drucker–Prager hybrid  
     GUDE   → Gudehus constitutive law (soil creep and consolidation)
